To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a new web-based tool called DoOPsearch, for searching in the conserved promoter motifs of chordate and plant genomes.
we developed a new web based tool for the analysis of conserved motifs in chordate and plant orthologous promoters.
we present a new tool for the comparative analysis of promoter regions of chordates and plants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of conserved regulatory elements in the promoter regions.
the identification and analysis of conserved transcription factor binding motifs from orthologous promoter sequences.
the identification of common conserved motifs from a broad taxonomic coverage and the analysis of their functional significance.

DoOPSearch is a useful web-based tool for the identification of common conserved motifs and for the subsequent analysis of the genes that are potentially involved in the regulation of a given biological function.
the DoOPSearch is an effective tool for the comparative genomics based identification of transcription factor binding sites and their target genes in chordate and plant species.
DoOPSearch is a web-based tool that can help in identifying the common motifs and their potential function in the promoter regions from chordate and plant species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide a web-based tool to search for common conserved motifs and to find genes with similar functions in the DoOP databases.
the DoOPSearch tool is a useful tool for the identification of common conserved motifs and the genes regulated by them in the promoter regions.

we provide the users with a new web-based tool for the analysis of conserved motifs in chordate or plant orthologous promoter sequences and we offer the users a new way for finding common motifs and genes that might be regulated by the same or similar transcription factors.

the comparative genomic analysis of orthologous promoters can reveal novel conserved motifs that might be important in gene regulation and that can help in the discovery of novel TFBSs.
